chmmc-2012-fall-individual-01.title: Factor
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-01.body:
$(5^{94}+5^{92})(2^{94}+2^{92})=5^{92}\cdot26\cdot2^{92}\cdot5=10^{92}\cdot130$, which is $13$ followed by $93$ zeros: two nonzero digits.

**Answer: 2**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-02.title: Multiples of $2013!$
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-02.body:
Every subset of $k\le2013$ elements has sum $2013!\cdot m$ for an integer $m$, and $k\mid2013!$, so the mean $\frac{2013!}{k}m$ is an integer. The $2013$ numbers $2013!\cdot i$ are distinct and positive.

**Answer: $A=\{2013!\cdot i: i=1,\dots,2013\}$**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-02.title: Any common multiple
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-02.body: More generally, take any distinct positive integers that are all multiples of $\operatorname{lcm}(1,2,\dots,2013)$; any such set works by the same argument.

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-03.title: Angles
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-03.body:
At $5{:}15$ the hour hand is at $157.5^\circ$ and the minute hand at $90^\circ$: the angle is $67.5^\circ$. The minute hand gains $5.5^\circ$ per minute. After $t$ minutes the hour hand is ahead by $67.5-5.5t$ degrees; this is $-67.5$ (the hands again $67.5^\circ$ apart, now with the minute hand ahead) when $5.5t=135$, $t=\frac{270}{11}\approx24.5$, which rounds to $25$ minutes.

**Answer: 25**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-04.title: Square both sides
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-04.body:
Let $u=\frac ab$. Then $1+\frac{a^2+3b^2}{2ab}=1+\frac u2+\frac3{2u}$ and the right side is $\sqrt{4+u+\frac3u}$. Put $w=u+\frac3u$. The equation is $1+\frac w2=\sqrt{4+w}$. Squaring, $1+w+\frac{w^2}4=4+w$, so $w^2=12$, $w=2\sqrt3$ (positive). Then $u+\frac3u=2\sqrt3$ gives $(u-\sqrt3)^2=0$, $u=\sqrt3$. So $a=\sqrt3\,b$ and with $a+b=1$, $b=\frac1{1+\sqrt3}$, $a=\frac{\sqrt3}{1+\sqrt3}=\frac{3-\sqrt3}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{3-\sqrt3}2$**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-05.title: Quadratic in $e^x$
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-05.body:
Let $t=e^x>0$: $t-\frac{12}t=4$, so $t^2-4t-12=0$, $(t-6)(t+2)=0$, $t=6$ (the root $-2$ is impossible). So $x=\ln6$, the only solution.

**Answer: $\ln 6$**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-06.title: Product of chord lengths
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-06.body:
With $\omega=e^{2\pi i/n}$, $\prod_{i<j}|\omega^i-\omega^j|=\sqrt{\prod_{i\ne j}|\omega^i-\omega^j|}=\sqrt{\prod_i|n\,\omega^{i(n-1)}|}=\sqrt{n^n}=n^{n/2}$ (using $\prod_{j\ne i}(\omega^i-\omega^j)=n\omega^{-i}$). This is rational iff $n$ is even (then it is an integer) or $n$ is an odd perfect square (then $\sqrt n$ is an integer; for non-square odd $n$, $n^{n/2}=n^{(n-1)/2}\sqrt n$ is irrational). Even $n\in[2,2013]$: $1006$. Odd squares $9,25,\dots,43^2=1849$ ($k=3,5,\dots,43$): $21$. Total $1006+21=1027$.

**Answer: 1027**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-07.title: Asymptotics
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-07.body:
$\sqrt{n^4+n^r}-n^2=\frac{n^r}{\sqrt{n^4+n^r}+n^2}$. For $r<4$ the denominator is $\sim2n^2$, so the terms are $\sim\frac12n^{r-2}$, and the series converges iff $r-2<-1$, i.e. $r<1$. For $r\ge4$ the terms do not tend to $0$ (each term is at least $(\sqrt2-1)n^2$), so the series diverges. So the series converges iff $r\in(-\infty,1)$, $a=1$.

**Answer: 1**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-08.title: Check
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-08.body:
$201^2+10^2=40401+100=40501$ and $199^2+30^2=39601+900=40501$. These were found by searching $a$ near $\sqrt{40501}\approx201.2$: $40501-a^2$ must be a perfect square for $a=201,200,\dots$; a complete search shows that these are the only two pairs.

**Answer: $(201,10)$ and $(199,30)$**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-09.title: Recurrence
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-09.body:
The level after day $n$ satisfies $k_n=0.99k_{n-1}+10$, $k_0=100$. Then $1000-k_n=0.99(1000-k_{n-1})$, so $1000-k_n=900\cdot0.99^n>0$ for all $n$. The level approaches $1000$ but never reaches it.

**Answer: never (forever)**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-10.title: Resultant trick
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-10.body:
$a_i^2-2=(a_i-\sqrt2)(a_i+\sqrt2)$, and $\prod_i(a_i-c)=\frac{P(c)}{2}$ (since $P(x)=2\prod(x-a_i)$ and the degree is even: $\prod(a_i-c)=\prod(c-a_i)=\frac{P(c)}2$). So the product is $\frac{P(\sqrt2)P(-\sqrt2)}{4}=\frac{P(\sqrt2)^2}4$ ($P$ is even). $P(\sqrt2)=2\cdot16+8-4+1=37$, so the value is $\frac{37^2}4=\frac{1369}4$.

**Answer: $\frac{1369}{4}$**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-11.title: Factor as a quartic
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-11.body:
Put $y=x^2+2x-5$. Then $-2x^2-3x+15=-2y+x+5$, so the equation is $y^2+2y=x+5$, i.e. $(y+1)^2=x+6$: $$(x^2+2x-4)^2-(x+6)=x^4+4x^3-4x^2-17x+10=0.$$ This factors as $(x^2+3x-2)(x^2+x-5)$ (multiply out to check). The roots of $x^2+3x-2$ are $\frac{-3\pm\sqrt{17}}2$ and those of $x^2+x-5$ are $\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{21}}2$.

**Answer: $x=\frac{-3\pm\sqrt{17}}2,\ \frac{-1\pm\sqrt{21}}2$**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-12.title: Law of cosines
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-12.body:
Since $x^2+y^2-2xy\cos120^\circ=x^2+y^2+xy$, place a point $O$ inside a triangle with segments $OA=x$, $OB=y$, $OC=z$ meeting at $120^\circ$ angles ($\angle AOB=\angle BOC=\angle COA=120^\circ$). Then $AB=3$, $BC=4$, $CA=5$: a right triangle of area $6$. The area is also $\frac12\sin120^\circ(xy+yz+zx)=\frac{\sqrt3}4(xy+yz+zx)$, so $xy+yz+zx=\frac{24}{\sqrt3}=8\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $8\sqrt3$**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-14.title: Euler product
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-14.body:
The squares in question are $3^{2i}5^{2j}7^{2k}$, $i,j,k\ge0$. The sum factors as a product of geometric series: $\frac1{1-\frac19}\cdot\frac1{1-\frac1{25}}\cdot\frac1{1-\frac1{49}}=\frac98\cdot\frac{25}{24}\cdot\frac{49}{48}=\frac{11025}{9216}$.

**Answer: $\frac{11025}{9216}$**

chmmc-2012-fall-individual-15.title: Search
chmmc-2012-fall-individual-15.body:
Write $y_1=1,y_2=b,y_3=c^2,y_4=d^3$ and $x_1=a,x_2=b,x_3=c,x_4=d$. The equations say $\sum_iy_ix_i^k=0$ for $k=0,1,2,3$. Group equal values among $a,b,c,d$ and let $Y_v$ be the sum of the $y_i$ with $x_i=v$. Then $\sum_vY_vv^k=0$ for $k=0,\dots,3$ over at most $4$ distinct values $v$, and the Vandermonde matrix is invertible, so every $Y_v=0$. The group of $a$ must have zero sum and contains $y_1=1$: the options are $\{a,b\}$: $1+v=0$; $\{a,c\}$: $1+v^2=0$ (no); $\{a,d\}$: $1+v^3=0$; $\{a,b,c\}$: $1+v+v^2=0$ (no); $\{a,b,d\}$: $1+v+v^3=0$ (no integer root); $\{a,c,d\}$: $1+v^2+v^3=0$ (no integer root); $\{a,b,c,d\}$: $(1+v)(1+v^2)=0$; $\{a\}$ alone: $1=0$ (no). So $a=-1$ and the group is $\{a,b\}$, $\{a,d\}$ or everything. Everything: $(-1,-1,-1,-1)$, which works. Group $\{a,b\}$ exactly: $b=-1$ and $c,d
e-1$; if $c
e d$ then $c^2=0=d^3$, a contradiction; if $c=d=t$ then $t^2+t^3=0$, so $t=0$: $(-1,-1,0,0)$. Group $\{a,d\}$ exactly: $d=-1$ and $b,c
e-1$; if $b
e c$ then $b=0=c^2$, a contradiction; if $b=c=t$ then $t+t^2=0$, so $t=0$: $(-1,0,0,-1)$. All three satisfy the system, so there are $3$ quadruples.

**Answer: 3**
